# Product

## Register

product

## Users

Writers, editors, researchers, and technically comfortable creators who want a focused drafting room with structured editorial feedback. They are usually trying to move from a vague brief or partial draft into a clearer manuscript, then export or publish it.

## Product Purpose

Twyne is a local-first writing desk with an AI-assisted room of editors. It helps writers define a project dossier, draft in rich text, receive persona feedback, score work against a rubric, manage citations, sync across devices when signed in, and publish or export finished work. Success means the writer keeps ownership and momentum while the product makes revision concrete.

## Brand Personality

Editorial, exacting, literary. The product should feel like a working writer's room rather than generic SaaS: opinionated, calm, and serious about craft without getting precious.

## Anti-references

Do not make Twyne look like a generic AI chat app, a growth dashboard, a blank note-taking clone, or a loud marketing funnel. Avoid decorative UI that competes with the manuscript, vague AI productivity claims, and controls that obscure where drafts and keys are stored.

## Design Principles

- Keep the manuscript central.
- Make data movement explicit: local, synced, published, or sent to a provider.
- Use standard controls for standard tasks, dressed in Twyne's editorial system.
- Prefer concise copy that names the actual action.
- Preserve writer trust through clear export, privacy, and account controls.

## Accessibility & Inclusion

Aim for WCAG AA contrast and keyboard-operable controls. Important interactions should work with semantic HTML where possible. Respect reduced-motion preferences, avoid color-only state, and keep long-form reading comfortable on mobile and desktop.
===README===
# Twyne

Twyne is a writer-first editing room. It opens with an anti-tabula-rasa interview so a draft starts from context instead of a blank page, then keeps that brief in front of every editor, judge, and margin note for the rest of the piece.

## Features

- Rich-text drafting with Tiptap, Qwik City, Vite, and Tailwind CSS.
- Anti-tabula-rasa project interview for title, format, audience, goal, tone, constraints, and success signal — with **typed follow-ups** (multiple choice, fill-in-the-blanks, scales) generated from what you've already said.
- A room of five editorial **personas** that read from your brief and draft and leave grounded feedback — and that **read along as you write**, not only when you ask.
- **Rubric** scoring gated on relevance: a Target Fit judge decides whether the draft is about the right thing, and caps the shape metrics when it isn't.
- **Voice**: hear each editor in their own voice, record spoken margin notes, and answer the interview out loud.
- **Citation detection** for URLs, DOIs, ISBNs, author-year citations, and footnote markers.
- **Comments** panel for review notes and threaded replies.
- **Apparatus** research panel (pluggable providers) for searching and pulling sources while writing.
- **Convex** backend for sync, with **Better Auth** (passkeys) sign-in and
  writer-owned **ATProto / Standard.site** publishing, including canonical
  Twyne readers and publication/document verification links.
- BYOK AI: bring your own key in Settings, stored in your browser and never sent to a server.
- Installable PWA with brand favicons and per-article OpenGraph share cards.

## The editorial room

Four panels sit beside the manuscript: **Cast** (the five editors), **Rubric**
(the galley proof), **Marginalia** (your notes), and **Apparatus** (sources).
Each tab carries an unread count, so work that arrives while you're looking
elsewhere isn't silent.

### The room reads as you write

Convening the room is deliberate and expensive — five model calls over the
whole manuscript. Alongside it, a background pass runs on a narrower brief:
once you've written **~300 net new words** _and_ stopped typing for **two
minutes**, all five editors read **only the new paragraphs**, plus a digest of
how the draft has been moving.

Those arrive as quieter "in passing" notes in the Cast panel. Two spend guards
sit on top — a five-minute floor between passes and a per-session cap — because
this runs without you asking. Turn it off with **Read as I write** in the room
settings.

The same digest goes along when you _do_ press Convene, so the deliberate pass
knows the trajectory rather than re-reading a cold snapshot.

### The rubric grades against _this_ piece

The static feature scorer measures shape — sentence-length variance,
type-token ratio, paragraph balance. It never reads the brief, so fluent prose
about the wrong subject used to score 10/10 on three categories.

A **Target Fit** judge now scores relevance independently of craft, and caps
every shape-derived criterion by it. Lowering target fit can only ever lower
the grade, never raise it.

The criteria themselves are yours to shape. Twyne ships a fixed spine so a
score in March means the same thing in June; you can disable or reweight any of
it, add criteria of your own ("stays in second person", "every section ends on
an image") for the room to judge, or ask it to **suggest criteria** fitted to
your format — proposals you accept, never applied silently. Customise anything
and a second "by your weights" score appears beside the editorial grade. Every
pass is recorded, so the panel shows the run of grades rather than a snapshot.

## Context

`src/components/landing/landing-page.tsx` currently carries the whole front page
in ~325 lines. It works, and two parts of it are genuinely good — the annotated
`WorkspacePreview` and the letterpress masthead/colophon — but the middle of the
page is its weak stretch: the `steps` array renders as four paragraphs of
unbroken prose in a `<ol>`, with no imagery anywhere on the page. Every visual
asset in `public/assets/` today is an SVG mark or a texture; there is not a
single photograph.

Motion is similarly thin. The only landing animation is `landing-rise` (a 0.7s
fade-and-rise, `global.css:2565`) applied to three hero elements. Nothing
responds to scroll.

This change gives the page real photographic plates, rebuilds the middle as a
magazine photo essay, and adds restrained scroll-driven motion — while keeping
the masthead, hero copy, workspace preview, CTA analytics wiring, and colophon
intact.

Direction confirmed with the user: **photographic desk plates**, **photo-essay
rebuild of the middle**, **editorial-restraint motion**.

## Assets — six generated plates

Codex image generation is verified working (`image_generation` feature is stable
and enabled; `codex login status` = logged in via ChatGPT). A test render into
the scratchpad produced an on-brand result: warm tungsten light, aged cream
manuscript, red proof marks on dark walnut.

Generate with, per image:

```
codex exec --sandbox workspace-write --skip-git-repo-check --cd <scratchpad> \
  "<prompt>" < /dev/null
```

Two flags matter and were found the hard way: `--skip-git-repo-check` (else it
refuses to run outside a trusted dir) and `< /dev/null` (else it blocks reading
stdin). Codex writes to `~/.codex/generated_images/<uuid>/…png` and copies to the
target path.

| Slug | Section | Subject | Native |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hero-desk` | full-bleed band under hero | whole writing desk overhead: manuscript pages fanned, red pencil, cold coffee ring, index cards, brass lamp pooling light | 1536×1024 → crop 3:1 |
| `plate-1-brief` | Step I, *Answer the brief* | open manila folder, typed index cards, fountain pen laid across | 1024×1536 |
| `plate-2-draft` | Step II, *Write the draft* | typewriter page half-written, stack of clean sheets, morning light | 1536×1024 |
| `plate-3-notes` | Step III, *Take the notes* | page dense with margin notes in five ink colours, five pencils fanned beside it | 1024×1536 |
| `plate-4-record` | Step IV, *Check the record* | library card-catalogue drawer pulled open, slips, books with paper bookmarks | 1536×1024 |
| `closing-stamp` | closing CTA | finished manuscript under a red approval stamp, hand just lifted away | 1024×1024 |

**Prompt discipline:** never ask for legible text. The test render's body copy came
out as convincing gibberish, which is exactly right — it reads as texture. Asking
for real words produces mangled letterforms. Each prompt ends with the shared
house style: *"muted warm tungsten light, shallow depth of field, aged cream
paper, vermilion red accents only, no legible text, no people's faces, no
modern electronics."*

throwaway script in the scratchpad — not committed, this is a one-shot pipeline:
crop to target aspect, resize to two widths, encode webp q78. Land them in a new
`public/assets/landing/` directory as `<slug>-760.webp` / `<slug>-1520.webp`
(plates) and `-1200/-2400` (hero band). Budget: ≤200KB for the largest variant of
each, ~1.2MB total. That is in line with what is already committed
(`hero-glow.png` is 241KB, `rubric-proof-fibers.png` 239KB).

Raster assets are referenced by URL from `public/`, matching
`src/global.css:1475` and `src/routes/rubric/index.tsx:127`. Only SVG marks use
the `~/media/assets/*.svg?jsx` inline-component path.

## Component changes

### `src/components/landing/landing-page.tsx`

Extend the existing `steps` array rather than replacing it — the copy is good and
should survive. Add `slug`, `alt`, and `side` (`"left" | "right"`) to each entry,
then render the `<ol>` as alternating spreads instead of a text list:

```
PLATE I    [image]  |  numeral + title + body
PLATE II   numeral + title + body  |  [image]
PLATE III  [image]  |  numeral + title + body
PLATE IV   numeral + title + body  |  [image]
```

Each spread carries a typewriter-font `PLATE I` caption above the title, matching
the existing `.dept-label` / `.landing-kicker` register. On mobile the grid
collapses to a single column, image first.

New pieces:
- A full-bleed hero band (`hero-desk`) between the hero copy and
  `WorkspacePreview`, with the slow ken-burns.
- The closing CTA sheet gets `closing-stamp` as a bleed image behind the existing
  `paper-sheet paper-foxed` treatment, with the `ImgApprovalStamp` SVG kept on top.
- A **mid-page CTA** after PLATE IV. `LandingCtaLocation`
  (`src/utils/product-analytics.ts:15`) already types `"mid_page"` and nothing in
  the codebase uses it — this wires up an analytics value that has been sitting
  unused.

`onStartBrief$` / `onSkipToEditor$` prop signatures and every existing call site
stay exactly as they are, so `src/routes/index.tsx` needs no change.

### Images markup

Explicit `width`/`height` (no CLS), `srcset`/`sizes` across the two widths,
`loading="lazy"` + `decoding="async"` on the plates, and `fetchpriority="high"`
with eager loading on the hero band only.

**Reveals — IntersectionObserver.** One observer, set up in a single
`useVisibleTask$({ strategy: "document-idle" })` in `LandingPage`, over
`[data-reveal]`, unobserving each element once revealed and disconnecting in
`cleanup`.

The start state must not be authored in plain CSS, or a JS failure would leave
the page permanently blank. Instead the same task sets `data-reveal-ready` on the
container, and CSS hides children only under that attribute:

```css
[data-reveal-ready] [data-reveal] { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(16px); }
[data-reveal].is-revealed        { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
```

No JS ⇒ nothing hidden ⇒ page reads exactly as it does today. This also keeps the
SSR'd HTML fully crawlable, which the recent `456fe34 fix: make public pages
crawlable` work cared about.

**Parallax and ken-burns — pure CSS, no JS.** Wrap in
`@supports (animation-timeline: view())` and drive the image drift off
`animation-timeline: view()`. Chrome/Edge/Safari get the effect; Firefox gets a
clean static image. This avoids adding a rAF scroll listener to a resumable Qwik
page for something purely decorative.

parallax on plate images; hero band 1.0 → 1.06 over 20s; 2px hover lift on plates.

**Reduced motion.** Add the new classes to a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`
block, following the nine that already exist in `global.css` (2322, 2448, 2586,
2854, 3344, 3814, 4531, 4712, 5148). Under reduce: no reveal hiding at all, no
parallax, no ken-burns, no hover lift. PRODUCT.md calls for exactly this.

## `src/global.css`

Append one commented block near the existing landing styles (~2565, after
`landing-rise`), reusing the established custom properties — `--color-paper-soft`,
`--color-ink`, `--color-vermilion`, `--font-typewriter`, `--font-display`,
`--shade`, `--emboss` — and the `color-mix(…)` idiom used throughout:

- `.landing-band` — full-bleed hero band, clipped, ken-burns inside
- `.landing-plate` — spread grid, alternating via `:nth-child(even)`
- `.landing-plate__figure` — framed image: 2px paper border, letterpress inset
  shadow, slight rotation matching `.stamp-tilt`'s vocabulary
- `.landing-plate__caption` — `PLATE I` in typewriter caps
- `.landing-reveal` — the fade/rise pair described above

**Theming.** Themes are attribute-based: `foolscap`, `broadsheet`, `nightpress`
(`global.css:180/204/230`). The photographs are warm and dark, so they sit
naturally on the default aged-newsprint palette. Two adjustments:
`[data-theme="nightpress"]` gets a slight `filter: brightness(0.92)` so plates
don't glare against `#191714`; `[data-theme="broadsheet"]` drops the paper-tone
overlay, since that preset is deliberately untinted (`global.css:222`).

## Verification

1. `bun run lint` and `bun run build.types` — must be clean.
2. `bun run dev.frontend` (Vite alone; the full `dev` script also spawns
   `convex dev`, which the landing page does not need).
3. Drive the running page with the `claude-in-chrome` tools: screenshot the full
   scroll at desktop width, then at 390px mobile, and confirm the spreads
   alternate, the plates reveal on scroll, and nothing overflows horizontally.
4. Toggle each of the three themes and re-screenshot the plate band.
5. Emulate `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` and confirm every plate is visible
   and static — the important failure mode, since a mistake here hides content.
6. Disable JavaScript and confirm the full page still renders (the
   `data-reveal-ready` guard).
7. `bun test` — no landing tests exist today
   (`src/utils/product-analytics.test.ts` is the only related file and does not
   touch the component), so this is a regression check, not a new-coverage claim.
8. Report the final byte total of `public/assets/landing/`.

## Out of scope

`WorkspacePreview` and its annotation slips are untouched. No masthead, hero
copy, or colophon changes. No new dependencies — `sharp` is already installed and
is used only at asset-build time, never shipped to the client.

---
name: codex-image-generation
description: How to generate Twyne's photographic assets with the codex CLI, plus the two flags that make it work non-interactively
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`codex exec` can generate images — the `image_generation` feature ships stable
and enabled (`codex features list | grep image_generation`), and auth is the
existing ChatGPT login (`codex login status`).

Two flags are required when driving it from a script, and neither is obvious:

```bash
codex exec --sandbox workspace-write --skip-git-repo-check --cd "$OUT" \
  "Use your built-in image generation tool to create ONE <aspect> image and
   save it as ./<slug>.png in the current directory. Subject: … Style: …
   Do not write code, do not install packages." < /dev/null
```

- **`--skip-git-repo-check`** — without it: *"Not inside a trusted directory"* and it exits.
- **`< /dev/null`** — without it, it blocks on *"Reading additional input from stdin"* even though a prompt was passed as an argument.

Codex writes to `~/.codex/generated_images/<uuid>/exec-<id>.png`, then copies to
the path you named. Sizes top out at **1536 on the long edge** (1024×1536,
1536×1024, 1024×1024) — plan crops around that, never upscale on disk.

**Prompt discipline:** never ask for legible text. Body copy renders as
convincing gibberish, which is exactly what you want for paper texture; asking
for real words produces mangled letterforms instead.

The house style that produced a coherent six-plate set for the landing page:
*muted warm tungsten light, shallow depth of field, aged cream paper, vermilion
as the only saturated accent, film grain, no legible text, no faces, no modern
electronics, no logos.* Output was genuinely on-brand for Twyne's editorial
register — dark walnut desks, aged manuscript, red proof marks.

Optimise with the already-installed `sharp` (v0.34.5). ESM can't resolve
`sharp` from a script outside the project — import it by absolute path
(`/home/diogenes/Projects/twyne/node_modules/sharp/lib/index.js`) or run the
script from inside the repo. webp q78 suits these photographs; drop to q68 for
dense handwriting, which compresses badly (232KB → 184KB with no visible loss).

**Why the reveal's hidden state is scoped to `[data-reveal-ready]`:** the
attribute is set only by the `useVisibleTask$` that installs the
IntersectionObserver. CSS hides `[data-reveal]` children *only* under that
attribute, so if JS never runs — or the reader asked for reduced motion, or
there's no IntersectionObserver — nothing is ever hidden and the SSR'd page
reads in full. Authoring the hidden state in plain CSS would have made a JS
failure blank the page, and would have broken the crawlability work in
`456fe34`. Don't "simplify" this by moving `opacity: 0` to a bare selector.

**Parallax is pure CSS** (`animation-timeline: view()` behind `@supports`), so
no rAF scroll listener is added to a resumable Qwik page. Firefox gets a static
photograph, which is fine.

Portrait plates get a narrower grid column (`0.66fr`) than landscape ones —
at half-width a 4:5 photograph towers over three lines of copy and opens a dead
gap. The `sizes` attribute differs per orientation to match.

`mid_page` in `LandingCtaLocation` (`src/utils/product-analytics.ts`) was typed
but unused before this; the CTA after PLATE IV now fires it.

Swapping a family is **not** a one-line change to `--font-display`. Five places

   a family `root.tsx` doesn't load means the writer sees it locally and their
   reader gets a fallback.
4. `src/utils/exchange.ts` — exported/printed HTML embeds its own font link and
   families, so exports keep the same identity.
5. `src/components/editor/manuscript-panel.tsx` — the menu's visible label.

Guarded by `typography-options.test.ts` ("every family the menu offers is one
the app actually loads") and `exchange-print.test.ts` ("loads every font family
the formatting menu can write"). Both hard-code the family list — update them.

currently a different face from the site.

Note Libre Baskerville ships only 400/700 (+400 italic) where Fraunces was

content.text:
All of it is in. Build clean, 1280 tests passing, 0 lint errors.

**Hero** — the photograph is now the hero itself, with a backdrop generated specifically with an empty walnut centre so type has ground to sit on. It's a fixed dark plate in all three themes (its cream is hard-coded, not themed, since the ground is dark everywhere). The headline rotates, typing out and then taking a copy-editor's rule through a word: *Start from ~~a blank page~~ a brief.* Headline 0 carries no correction deliberately — it's what SSR, crawlers and `aria-label` get, so it has to read as a clean sentence.

**Photos** — all six regenerated weathered and askew: foxing, frayed deckled edges, dog-eared corners, water rings, sheets dropped at angles. Plate 3 needed a second pass; the first weathered version lost the five-colour annotation that carried its meaning.

**Scatter** — each plate has its own tilt and drift from the data, and they fall in over-rotated and settle, with the easing overshooting so they touch down. Hover picks one up off the pile.

**Type** — Libre Baskerville replaced Fraunces. That wasn't a one-line change: `typography-options.ts` offers Fraunces to *writers* as a manuscript font, and its own comment says the menu must only list fonts `root.tsx` loads. Two tests enforce it. So the swap covers the font link, the token, the writer's menu, the export/print stylesheet, and the editor label.

**Three things worth flagging:**

The strike-through and caret being invisible was **my bug, not the photograph**. When I swapped the band CSS for the hero, my replacement range swallowed the entire rotator block — `.landing-rotator__struck`, the caret, and the typed-heading rules were all deleted from `global.css`. Nothing was being styled at all. Restored, with brighter mark colours since the page vermilion goes muddy on near-black.

**I found and fixed a real 0.042 CLS.** `.landing-hero` centres with `place-items: center`, which also makes the grid item size to its *content* — the block was 729px against the fallback face and 768px once the webfont landed, sliding the whole hero sideways on every load. Page CLS is now 0.033, down from 0.058. The remainder is `font-display: swap` reflow plus tiny per-keystroke re-centring of the centred headline; both were characteristics the site already had.

**OG share cards are still Fraunces.** `og-image.ts` renders them server-side from two committed `.ttf` binaries under `assets/og/`. Switching them needs Libre Baskerville TTF cuts downloaded and committed — I haven't done that, since downloading files is something I'd want you to okay first. Say the word and I'll fetch them from Google Fonts; until then share cards are a different face from the site.

One thing I'd still push back on gently: the rotating headline means the h1 text changes continuously, and I've pinned the accessible name to headline 0. That's the right call for screen readers, but it does mean two of your three headlines are invisible to them and to crawlers.
